strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: user-level private federated ASR with large transformers, heterogeneous speaker data, and domain mismatch between public pretraining and federated adaptation.

The strongest contribution is empirical. In Table 1, per-layer clipping reduces English test WER from 31.1% to 20.4% at the same noise setting and total clipping bound. This demonstrates substantial value from revisiting an existing technique.

The experimental study covers three languages and systematically investigates initialization, cohort size, data heterogeneity, optimizers, and augmentation. Reusing configurations across languages provides useful evidence of training robustness.

Public datasets, detailed preprocessing and training configurations, pseudocode, compute reporting, and a code link support reproducibility. The manuscript explicitly discloses its population extrapolation and public-seed assumptions; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The advertised convergence rate does not follow from the stated conditions. Corollary 1 requires κ = 1 − 8(1 − η_loc T_loc)^2 > 0 while prescribing η_loc = Θ(1/(L√(T_loc T))). For fixed T_loc, this makes κ tend to −7 as T increases. Consequently, the asymptotic convergence claim and corresponding recovery of prior rates in Appendix F.7 are unsupported.

The convergence proof contains additional unjustified steps. Equations (33)–(34) treat LAMB's preconditioner p_h^(t) as independent of the current DP noise, although equations (10)–(15) construct it from the same noisy update. The factorization and elimination of noise cross terms therefore require a different argument. Equation (20) also infers uniformly bounded gradients from smoothness using an unstated compact-domain assumption.

The headline privacy–utility combinations are projections rather than jointly demonstrated results. At the relevant noise levels, the actual English experiments use 1,024 clients per round from 34,753 speakers and report ε around 10^7–10^8. The ε = 4.5 and 7.2 results instead assume 204,800-client cohorts and populations of approximately 7 million and 70 million while retaining the measured WER. This assumption is honestly disclosed, but non-private scaling experiments up to 5,120 clients do not validate utility under the projected private-training regime.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed essential interaction between LAMB and per-layer clipping. Tables 8–9 compare optimizers without DP; a matched private-training comparison crossing optimizer choice with clipping strategy is missing. Optimizer stability parameters are also left at defaults despite cited evidence that they matter. Together with the single architecture, marginal clipping gains on French/German, and absent repeated-run uncertainty estimates, this limits the broader claims about large-model optimization.
